ambiguous.why: ISC2 CC teaches ransomware as the canonical denial-of-access/availability event, and that is the answer I grade. But a student who has read about modern double-extortion ransomware can argue Confidentiality (data is also stolen and leaked), and a student reasoning literally can argue Integrity (the bytes on disk were altered without authorisation). The stem does not mention exfiltration, so Availability is the defensible primary, but the deliberation is real.

Backups are the textbook availability control, and in a ransomware scenario they are what makes records reachable again — so IN. A student can fairly argue that the word 'immutable' is specifically an integrity property (write-once, unalterable), making this a control whose *primary* purpose is protecting the trustworthiness of the copy. I grade the recovery purpose, not the word.

ambiguous.item: Separation of duties on payment approvals
ambiguous.why: Separation of duties is a management/administrative control in ISC2 CC — it is a rule about how work is divided, established by policy. A student can argue that in practice it is enforced by the ERP's approval workflow and is therefore technical. I grade the control's nature, not its enforcement mechanism, so IN.

ambiguous.item: You decline to exaggerate a threat in a sales pitch to frighten a prospect into buying
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.alternative: Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
ambiguous.why: The act itself is refusing to be dishonest, which is squarely Canon II. But ISC2's own Canon IV guidance warns against sensationalism and 'FUD' selling because it damages the reputation of the profession, and several study guides use exactly this scenario as a Canon IV illustration. Textbook-dependent; I would accept a well-argued Canon IV.

ambiguous.item: A client pressures you to overstate their security posture in an audit report, and you refuse
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.alternative: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
ambiguous.why: Falsifying a report is a truthfulness failure, so Canon II. A student can argue Canon III on the grounds that the conflict is with a principal and ISC2's Canon III guidance covers not letting a principal's pressure compromise honest work; a stronger student could even reach for Canon I if third parties rely on the audit. I had to deliberate here.
